verdict: Second read agrees with the first: this essay is clean and close to the mature register. Literal search finds no forbidden word, no em-dash, no exclamation point, no connective filler, no title, years, book count or denomination, and no one-directional politics. Two of the seven findings survive. The other five were 'consider' items whose replacements either changed a claim, removed content, or sanded off plain signposting that the brief lists as one of his habits. Nothing new was found on the second pass.

keep.quote: Jesus didn't despise the man's goodness. He told him the one thing he lacked, which was to sell what he had, give to the poor, and come and follow him.
keep.tell: Paragraph opener that restates the paragraph before it
keep.why: The previous paragraph already says 'By any ordinary measure he was a good man. Jesus did not dispute it,' and then quotes Mark 10:21. 'Jesus didn't despise the man's goodness' makes the same point a third time in the same 'Jesus did not / Jesus didn't' frame. Checked against the ledger: the paraphrase of Mark 10:21 is untouched.
keep.replacement: Then he told him the one thing he lacked, which was to sell what he had, give to the poor, and come and follow him.

keep.quote: The hope of the gospel is that the only one who is good came looking for people who were not.
keep.why: The last three lines of the essay each open with a label ('The question is', 'there is a second question', 'The hope of the gospel is that'). The sentence under the third label is the strongest in the essay and Luke 19:10 follows it immediately, so the caption is not needed. No other essay on the shelf uses the phrase, so this is a small gain, not a stamp; James may prefer to keep the label as a courtesy that marks the line as Christian confession.
keep.replacement: The only one who is good came looking for people who were not.

dropped: "That isn't a proof, and Christians shouldn't sell it as one. It is a question about which account makes better sense of what all of us already know." Dropped: the replacement ('But it does make better sense') turns a question left open for the skeptic into an assertion, which changes the claim. The concession is his voice and the two antitheses in the section do different work.

"It's a real objection, and the answer is that every account stops somewhere, as Wielenberg himself argues." Dropped: plain signposting after a voiced objection is a habit the brief names as his; a reader hears a person answering, not a machine.
"He presses until it hurts:" Dropped: a spoken, slightly rough phrase that introduces Romans 2:21; not a machine pattern, and 'He keeps pressing' is flatter without being more his.

"Paul's argument arrives where it was heading from the start:" Dropped: it tells the reader that Romans 3:23 is the conclusion of the Romans 1 to 2 argument, which is real work; the replacement adds 'in the next chapter' and I would not stake the essay on the change.

"a Christian who is cruel, dishonest or contemptuous of unbelievers" Dropped: 'dishonest' is not filler; it answers 'more truthful' in the opening section and 'do you not teach yourself' in the verse just quoted. Cutting it removes content.
for_james: You appear in one sentence: 'I was an atheist before I was a Christian, so the person on the other side of this question is someone I used to be.' It is used well. If you remember what you thought, as an atheist, when a Christian told you that you couldn't be good without God, one or two true sentences there would make the essay unmistakably yours. None has been invented.

The two Nietzsche sentences are Walter Kaufmann's translation, confirmed by search matches and not from the book. If you own The Portable Nietzsche, check pages 515 to 516; the ledger holds the public-domain Ludovici wording as an alternative.
